However, other evidence complicates this single-factor narrative — marine strata studies confirm significant volcanic carbon emissions during the PETM , yet the onset coincides with a mercury low, suggesting at least one other carbon reservoir was involved top candidates for the primary trigger also include methane release from ocean sediments or permafrost

Overall, while volcanic activity clearly contributed to the event, the scientific consensus leans toward a nuanced scenario involving multiple interacting factors rather than a single definitive trigger

claim_details.claim: The link between yerba mate and cancer is disputed in the scientific literature. Some epidemiological studies have found an association between very hot yerba mate consumption and increased risks of esophageal, head and neck bladder cancers, with PAHs in the tea and high drinking temperature identified as potential contributing factors. However, other research has argued that the elevated cancer risk is primarily attributable to temperature rather than the tea itself, noting that drinking any very hot liquid may increase esophageal cancer risk regardless of the beverage type. Additionally, yerba mate has also been shown to possess anti-cancer properties in laboratory settings, capable of inducing cell death in certain cancer models, though this has not been confirmed in human studies. Overall, while some evidence suggests a possible risk when consumed very hot in large quantities, the consensus is that the traditional beverage itself is unlikely to cause cancer under normal conditions the strongest risk factor appears to be temperature

match_details.gold_answer: Association exists but is conditional — hot yerba mate is linked to elevated risk of esophageal, oral, and laryngeal cancers primarily due to temperature (thermal damage) and PAH content, especially when combined with tobacco/alcohol; at lower temperatures the risk is not clearly elevated; yerba mate also shows anti-cancer properties in lab settings.
